propositions.text: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large knife demanded money from a store worker.
propositions.quote: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large, butcher-style knife came into a variety store and demanded money.

propositions.text: The robber's actions were caught on security camera.
propositions.quote: His actions were caught by the store’s security camera.

paragraphs.summary: A man in a blue Halloween mask with a large knife robbed a store, caught on security camera.

propositions.text: Police found items including a blue mask, a large knife, and a cash register cover.
propositions.quote: The police found a blue Halloween mask, a large knife, and a plastic cover from the store’s cash register.

propositions.text: DNA testing matched the mask to Marty David O’Brien with a very low probability of unrelated match.
propositions.quote: A test of the DNA found on the blue mask matched only one person: Marty David O’Brien.

paragraphs.summary: Police found items including a mask and knife; DNA matched O’Brien with a very low chance of unrelated match.

propositions.text: O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.

paragraphs.summary: O’Brien was charged and convicted of robbery and other offences.

propositions.text: At trial, nine witnesses testified; the investigating officer mentioned O’Brien’s prior record.
propositions.quote: Nine witnesses testified; the investigating officer made brief references to Mr. O’Brien’s prior criminal record.

propositions.text: The defence did not object to the character evidence nor request it be limited.
propositions.quote: There was no objection to this evidence by the defence nor any request that it be limited.

propositions.text: The defence used the character evidence in cross-examination.
propositions.quote: the defence used the evidence in its cross-examination of the investigating officer.

propositions.text: The defence only referred to O’Brien’s reputation as a “known offender” in closing.
propositions.quote: Only defence counsel, in closing submissions, referred again to Mr. O’Brien’s reputation as a “known offender”.

propositions.text: The Crown did not mention the character evidence in its closing.
propositions.quote: The Crown made no mention of the character evidence in its closing submission.

propositions.text: The trial judge made no reference to the character evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge made no reference of any kind to it.

propositions.text: O’Brien did not testify; no evidence was called by the defence.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien did not testify and the defence called no evidence.

paragraphs.summary: At trial, character evidence was admitted without objection; the defence used it in cross, but not in closing; the judge made no reference.

propositions.text: O’Brien appealed on the basis that the verdict was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The basis of Mr. O’Brien’s appeal to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal was that the verdict was unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court asked counsel to address character evidence, though it was not a ground of appeal.
propositions.quote: the clerk of the court, at the panel’s request, wrote to counsel and asked that they be prepared to address the issue of character evidence.

propositions.text: O’Brien had not raised the character evidence issue in his appeal documents.
propositions.quote: Mr. O’Brien had not raised this issue as a ground of appeal either in his notice of appeal or his factum.

paragraphs.summary: O’Brien appealed on reasonableness; court asked about character evidence despite it not being a ground of appeal.

propositions.text: The Crown acknowledged it was an error for the trial judge not to exclude or qualify the character evidence.
propositions.quote: The Crown acknowledged that it was an error for the trial judge not to exclude the character evidence or qualify its purpose.

propositions.text: The Crown argued the error was not serious enough to prevent applying the curative proviso.
propositions.quote: but submitted that since it was not a serious error, the curative proviso in s. 686(1) (b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , should be applied.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown admitted the trial judge erred in allowing character evidence but argued it was not a serious error.

propositions.text: All three judges found the verdict was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: All three judges concluded that the verdict was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: The majority found the trial judge made a serious error in allowing character evidence.
propositions.quote: The majority held, however, that the trial judge made a serious error in allowing the character evidence to be heard.

propositions.text: The majority believed the judge did not disabuse himself of the character evidence.
propositions.quote: there was no indication that he “disabused himself from that evidence or was otherwise aware that it could not be considered”

propositions.text: The Crown failed to show the judge was not influenced by the character evidence.
propositions.quote: The Crown had, as a result, not discharged its onus of demonstrating that the judge was not influenced, “consciously or unconsciously”, by the impugned prejudicial evidence.

propositions.text: The appeal was allowed and a new trial ordered.
propositions.quote: The appeal was allowed and a new trial ordered.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge would have dismissed the appeal.
propositions.quote: The dissenting judge, Fichaud J.A., would have dismissed the appeal.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge believed the error was not serious and caused no miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: In his view, the error in hearing the investigating officer’s propensity evidence was not a serious one and caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge believed the reasons showed the improper evidence had no impact.
propositions.quote: He concluded: The trial judge’s written reasons satisfy me affirmatively that the improper evidence had no impact.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge believed the Crown’s burden was satisfied.
propositions.quote: This, in my view, satisfies the Crown’s burden under the proviso.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge believed the curative proviso was available.
propositions.quote: The judge’s words that he relied “entirely on the DNA evidence.”

propositions.text: The dissenting judge shared the view that the appeal should be allowed.
propositions.quote: I share this view.

paragraphs.summary: The majority found the error serious and ordered a new trial; the dissent believed the error was harmless and would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: The issue was whether the trial judge’s error was harmless or outside the curative proviso.
propositions.quote: The issue before us was whether the trial judge’s error in hearing “bad character” evidence — and his related failure to specifically address that evidence in his reasons — was a harmless one, or whether it was outside the borders of the curative proviso.

paragraphs.summary: The court considered whether the error was harmless or outside the curative proviso.

propositions.text: At trial, the only issue was identification.
propositions.quote: At trial, the only issue was identification.

propositions.text: The trial judge carefully approached the evidence and linked the blue mask to the robbery.
propositions.quote: The trial judge cautioned himself about the need to approach such evidence with care, then concluded... that the blue mask was associated with the robbery.

propositions.text: The judge’s findings did not rely on the character evidence.
propositions.quote: The investigating officer’s character evidence played no role in this finding.

paragraphs.summary: The trial focused on identification; the judge carefully linked the mask to the crime without relying on character evidence.

propositions.text: The DNA evidence was the key to linking O’Brien to the mask.
propositions.quote: The question then becomes whether the mask is connected to the accused, to Mr. O’Brien beyond a reasonable doubt, and that depends, as I have indicated, entirely on the DNA evidence.

propositions.text: The judge concluded the DNA “clearly ties” O’Brien to the mask.
propositions.quote: The judge observed: The question then becomes whether the mask is connected to the accused, to Mr. O’Brien beyond a reasonable doubt, and that depends, as I have indicated, entirely on the DNA evidence.

propositions.text: The judge found the DNA established O’Brien’s identity as the robber.
propositions.quote: the DNA evidence establishes the accused’s identity as the robber beyond a reasonable doubt.

paragraphs.summary: DNA evidence was the sole basis for linking O’Brien to the mask and the robbery.

propositions.text: The character evidence did not influence the convictions.
propositions.quote: The propensity evidence from the investigating officer clearly played no part in the convictions.

propositions.text: The judge relied entirely on DNA evidence, as confirmed by detailed reasons.
propositions.quote: not only did the trial judge expressly state that he relied entirely on the DNA evidence to identify Mr. O’Brien, his detailed reasons confirm this exclusive reliance.

propositions.text: Express reliance on DNA evidence means no unfairness or miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: when a trial judge expressly arrives at a conclusion on the critical issue “independently of the inadmissible evidence . . . no unfairness can be said to arise, nor has there been a miscarriage of justice”.

paragraphs.summary: The judge’s explicit statement of reliance on DNA evidence indicates the character evidence did not influence the verdict.

propositions.text: The judge’s reasons show he relied “entirely” on DNA evidence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said in his reasons that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence.

propositions.text: Imputing reliance on character evidence contradicts the judge’s reasons.
propositions.quote: Imputing such reliance into reasons that state the contrary creates a new, unchartable universe of appellate review.

propositions.text: Judges should base review on reasons, not speculation.
propositions.quote: trial judges should not be held to some “abstract standard of perfection”.

propositions.text: The judge’s reasons are trustworthy and show no subconscious bias.
propositions.quote: The chain of fact, law and logic in this case was impeccable. I see nothing about his approach that suggests a subconscious subversion.

paragraphs.summary: The reasons demonstrate the judge relied solely on DNA evidence, and reasons should be trusted over speculation about unarticulated thoughts.

propositions.text: The judge was entitled to rely on his reasons and they were well-founded.
propositions.quote: The trial judge was entitled to be taken at his word. His chain of fact, law and logic in this case was impeccable.

propositions.text: There is no indication of subconscious bias in the judge’s approach.
propositions.quote: nothing about his approach that suggests a subconscious subversion of his articulated thoughts.

paragraphs.summary: The judge’s reasons are trustworthy and show no subconscious bias, supporting the conclusion that reliance on DNA evidence was proper.

propositions.text: The court agrees the error was harmless and caused no miscarriage of justice.
propositions.quote: I therefore agree with Fichaud J.A. that the admission of the improper character evidence was a harmless error that caused no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The court would allow the appeal and restore the convictions.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal and restore the convictions.

propositions.text: The dissenting judge would have dismissed the appeal.
propositions.quote: The reasons of Binnie and LeBel JJ. were delivered by Binnie J. (dissenting) — I. Introduction

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the character evidence error harmless; the appeal should be allowed, restoring convictions; dissenting judge would dismiss appeal.

propositions.text: The DNA evidence was the sole basis for the conviction, not the propensity evidence, which played no part.
propositions.quote: not only did the trial judge expressly state that he relied entirely on the DNA evidence to identify Mr. O’Brien, his detailed reasons confirm this exclusive reliance.

propositions.text: When a trial judge relies solely on admissible evidence, no unfairness or miscarriage of justice arises.
propositions.quote: when a trial judge expressly arrives at a conclusion on the critical issue “independently of the inadmissible evidence . . . no unfairness can be said to arise, nor has there been a miscarriage of justice”

paragraphs.summary: The DNA evidence was the only basis for conviction; propensity evidence did not influence the outcome, supporting no miscarriage of justice.

propositions.text: The Crown uses DNA evidence to support convictions from an unfair trial, as agreed by Nova Scotia Court of Appeal judges.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Crown invokes the magic of DNA evidence to salvage convictions obtained in what all the judges of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal agreed was an unfair trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown relies on DNA evidence to uphold convictions from an allegedly unfair trial, as acknowledged by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: The respondent was convicted of a convenience store robbery; identification was the only issue; DNA was the only evidence linking him.
propositions.quote: The only live issue was identification. There was no evidence, circumstantial or otherwise, linking him to the crime except for traces of DNA on one of two masks.

paragraphs.summary: The case centered on identification, with DNA evidence as the sole link to the respondent, and no other evidence connecting him to the crime.

propositions.text: The trial judge admitted propensity evidence without comment or indication of recognizing its unfairness.
propositions.quote: The trial judge let in the propensity evidence without comment and gave no hint in his reasons that he recognized that the police branding of the respondent as a career criminal was against basic principles of trial fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge admitted propensity evidence without acknowledging its potential unfairness, raising concerns about trial fairness.

propositions.text: The respondent is entitled to a trial where the judge recognizes the danger of propensity evidence; the reasons do not show this.
propositions.quote: The respondent, now sentenced to six years and six months in prison, is entitled to know that the trial judge recognized the danger of propensity evidence and consciously put it aside.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent's right to a fair trial was compromised as the judge's reasons do not demonstrate awareness of the propensity evidence's dangers.

propositions.text: Majority judges consider the word 'entirely' sufficient to dismiss the unfairness; the dissent disagrees, citing trial context and DNA issues.
propositions.quote: A majority of my colleagues conclude that the trial judge’s use of the word “entirely” in relation to his reliance on the DNA evidence is enough to render the unfairness of the trial harmless.

paragraphs.summary: The court debates whether the judge's reliance on the word 'entirely' on DNA evidence dismisses the trial's unfairness, with differing opinions.

propositions.text: Crown's evidence aimed to portray respondent as a 'bad person'; police testimony included inadmissible propensity evidence.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s evidence at trial sought to portray the respondent as a “bad person” of the sort likely to commit the robbery of a convenience store.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown presented evidence suggesting the respondent's bad character, including inadmissible propensity evidence from police testimony.

propositions.text: The evidence of bad character was inadmissible; its admission made the trial unfair, as per previous case law.
propositions.quote: Both the majority and the minority in the court below found the evidence of bad character to be wholly inadmissible and the trial on that account to be unfair.

paragraphs.summary: The inadmissible bad character evidence was deemed to have compromised the fairness of the trial.

propositions.text: Identification evidence included a witness about a red car and DNA evidence from masks.
propositions.quote: The identification of the respondent as the perpetrator rested on two strands of evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Identification relied on a witness about a red car and DNA evidence from masks.

propositions.text: Witness testimony about a red car was unhelpful; DNA evidence matched respondent's DNA on masks.
propositions.quote: The trial judge correctly concluded that the “red car” evidence was essentially unhelpful.

paragraphs.summary: Red car evidence was unhelpful; DNA evidence matched respondent's DNA on masks, but did not prove guilt alone.

propositions.text: DNA match shows contact, not guilt; it does not prove the respondent committed the robbery.
propositions.quote: Evidence of a “match” does not, of course, prove guilt of the offence.

paragraphs.summary: DNA matching indicates contact but does not establish that the respondent committed the robbery.

propositions.text: The trial judge relied entirely on DNA to link respondent to the mask, but a logical leap is needed to connect this to the robbery.
propositions.quote: The trial judge said that he relied “entirely” on the DNA evidence to link the respondent to the mask, which the trial judge concluded (on other evidence) was the mask used in the robbery.

paragraphs.summary: The judge's reliance on DNA alone to connect respondent to the mask involves a logical leap to the actual robbery.

propositions.text: Section 686(1)(b)(iii) allows upholding convictions despite legal errors if no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice occurred.
propositions.quote: Section 686(1) (b)(iii) permits an appellate court to uphold a conviction despite error of law committed by the trial judge where that error has not led to a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Section 686(1)(b)(iii) permits affirming convictions despite legal errors if no substantial injustice resulted.

propositions.text: The proviso applies only if the outcome would have been the same; the Crown bears the burden of proof.
propositions.quote: The “curative proviso” is to be applied only in those cases where the outcome of the trial, irrespective of the error, would necessarily have been the same.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown must prove on a balance of probabilities that the legal error was harmless for the proviso to apply.

propositions.text: The Crown must show the legal error was harmless, either through no prejudice or overwhelming evidence.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may be applied, according to its modern interpretation, where the Crown can establish on a balance of probabilities that the legal error is harmless, in the sense that no prejudice has resulted, or that, despite any prejudice caused by the trial judge’s error of law, the evidence against the accused is so overwhelming that a trier of fact would inevitably convict.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown must demonstrate that the legal error caused no prejudice or that evidence was overwhelming for conviction.

propositions.text: Relying on the judge's silence on inadmissible evidence is insufficient; 'entirely' does not imply distancing from propensity evidence.
propositions.quote: In the application of the curative proviso on the facts of this case, I do not think that it is sufficient to rely on the trial judge’s silence on the issues of the inadmissible police evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that silence on inadmissible evidence does not suffice; 'entirely' does not indicate the judge disavowed propensity evidence.

propositions.text: The Crown bears the burden of proving harmlessness; the court does not attribute flawed reasoning to the judge based on speculation.
propositions.quote: My concern does not “impute” flawed reasoning to the trial judge on the basis of “speculative imagination” (reasons of Abella J., at paras. 16-17).

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes that the Crown bears the burden of proving harmlessness and avoids speculative reasoning about the judge's intent.

propositions.text: Respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the judge's acceptance of DNA; Crown responds the judge was unaware of this evidence.
propositions.quote: The respondent argues that the evidence of bad character was prejudicial because it predisposed the trial judge to uncritical acceptance of the DNA evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent claims bad character evidence prejudiced the judge; the Crown counters the judge was unaware of this evidence.

propositions.text: The Crown says the judge was unaffected because he did not mention bad character evidence in reasons; the judge was unaware of the problem.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s response is that the trial judge was not affected by the evidence of bad character because he didn’t mention it in his reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the judge was unaffected by bad character evidence as he did not mention it, implying unawareness.

propositions.text: Majority declined to apply the curative proviso due to lack of other evidence linking respondent to the crime; some cases differ.
propositions.quote: In this case, the majority in the Court of Appeal declined to apply the curative proviso in part because there was no other evidence linking the respondent to the crime.

paragraphs.summary: The appellate court declined to apply the proviso, citing absence of additional evidence linking respondent to the crime.

propositions.text: DNA on mask is like a fingerprint; its probative value depends on other evidence linking the accused to the crime.
propositions.quote: The presence of the appellant’s DNA on the mask is equivalent to a fingerprint. The Crown’s expert testified that only small amounts of DNA are sufficient, and can be present for years.

paragraphs.summary: DNA evidence on the mask is similar to a fingerprint; its significance depends on other evidence linking the accused to the crime.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s reasons failed to address problematic police evidence, which is a deficiency that cannot be dismissed as harmless.
propositions.quote: The failure of the trial judge’s reasons to address the problematic police evidence is a deficiency that cannot simply be brushed off.

propositions.text: The Crown argues trial judges are presumed to know the law, but this was rejected in R. v. Sheppard.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that trial judges are presumed to know the law. However, the argument that important deficiencies in trial reasons can be excused on the basis that trial judges are presumed to know the law was rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge's failure to address police evidence is a serious deficiency, rejecting the Crown's presumption argument.

propositions.text: There is a significant difference between inadmissible police opinion evidence in Leaney and prejudicial bad character evidence.
propositions.quote: There is a significant difference between appellate tolerance of inadmissible opinion evidence in circumstances where the trial judge found that the opinion evidence was unnecessary... and prejudicial evidence of bad character.

propositions.text: In Leaney, police opinion evidence was unobjectionable and considered surplusage, unlike here where the information itself is objectionable.
propositions.quote: The content of the officers’ testimony in Leaney was itself unobjectionable. The problem was that it was not their place to utter it.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes Leaney's police evidence as surplusage, unlike the prejudicial character evidence here.

propositions.text: The Crown should not benefit from the curative proviso because the trial reasons showed no awareness of police testimony issues.
propositions.quote: The Crown should not have the benefit of the curative proviso because the trial judge’s reasons demonstrated no awareness of the problem of the police testimony.

propositions.text: In R. v. Rahm, the trial judge understood that bad character evidence was inadmissible unless placed in issue.
propositions.quote: During the course of the trial, the trial judge made it clear that he understood that bad character was not admissible where character had not been placed in issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the trial judge's lack of awareness of police testimony issues disqualifies the curative proviso.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s error of law cannot be dismissed as harmless, and a new trial is warranted unless the error is proven harmless.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that the trial judge’s error of law can be dismissed as “harmless”, and... the respondent is entitled to a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the error of law is not harmless, entitling the respondent to a new trial.

propositions.text: The curative proviso can be applied if the case against the accused is overwhelming despite an error of law.
propositions.quote: The curative proviso may also be applied when, despite an error of law that is not harmless, the case against an accused is so overwhelming that a guilty verdict would be the only reasonable outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the circumstances under which the curative proviso may be used.

propositions.text: The Crown did not argue that its case was so strong that conviction was inevitable, which was correct.
propositions.quote: The Crown did not even argue that its case was so strong that a trier of fact would inevitably convict.

propositions.text: It is rare to deny a new trial based on conjecture that an error was harmless or that guilt is overwhelming.
propositions.quote: It is an exceptional thing to deny an accused the new trial to which he is otherwise entitled because of an appellate court’s conjecture that the error was “harmless” or that any reasonable trier of fact, properly instructed, would simply find the evidence of guilt to be overwhelming.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Crown did not claim its case was overwhelming, which is rare and significant.

propositions.text: Denying a new trial based on conjecture that an error was harmless is exceptional.
propositions.quote: It is an exceptional thing to deny an accused the new trial to which he is otherwise entitled because of an appellate court’s conjecture that the error was “harmless” or that any reasonable trier of fact, properly instructed, would simply find the evidence of guilt to be overwhelming.

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes that denying a new trial based on presumed harmless error is exceptional.

propositions.text: The Crown's burden to invoke the curative proviso is higher than proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The burden on the Crown seeking to invoke the curative proviso “is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case ‘beyond a reasonable doubt’ at trial”.

propositions.text: The evidence must be so overwhelming that conviction is inevitable or would invariably result, a higher standard than proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: The standard applied by an appellate court, namely that the evidence against an accused is so overwhelming that conviction is inevitable or would invariably result, is a substantially higher one than the requirement that the Crown prove its case “beyond a reasonable doubt” at trial.

propositions.text: The Crown cannot establish that its case was overwhelming.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Crown cannot establish that its case against the respondent was “overwhelming”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown faces a higher standard to invoke the curative proviso and cannot meet it here.

propositions.text: The court agrees the curative proviso does not apply and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: I agree with the majority opinion in the court below that the curative proviso has no application, and accordingly I would dismiss the appeal.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed, with Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.
propositions.quote: Appeal allowed, Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agreeing the curative proviso does not apply, with dissenting judges.
